content_preview.title: Male Sperm Whales' Slow Clicks Are the Loudest Communication Signals of Any Mammal, Aarhus Study Finds
content_preview.summary: A study led by Aarhus University finds male sperm whales' slow clicks exceed 200 dB and can carry up to 70 kilometers, the loudest mammalian communication signal recorded.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Male sperm whales produce slow, low-frequency clicks that register as the loudest communication signal of any mammal, according to a study from researchers at Aarhus University published in the *Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences*, as reported by [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-08-male-sperm-whales-loudest-communication.html). The paper, titled "Extreme Rhythm Keeping in Long-Range Slow Click Communication of Sperm Whales," appears in Volume 1559, Issue 1, Article e702...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-structured Briefing (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know), 564 words, within the 300-800 Briefing range. Neutral, factual tone throughout — no sensationalism, no AI self-reference. Note one minor stylistic wrinkle: the 'What We Don't Know' bullet embeds the abstract's clause '"may be achieved by the sperm whales using extrinsic echo information from the environment to maintain extreme isochrony"' after 'The study abstract speculates that whales,' which reads slightly awkwardly grammatically (a passive-voice quote spliced onto an active-voice lead-in) but does not misrepresent the source and is a verbatim quote, not a paraphrase — a style nit, not a factual or sourcing defect, so it does not rise to a corrections-worthy issue.
editor_notes.source_verification: Two sources, both read in full. (1) pure.au.dk/portal snapshot (source-1.html.gz, sha256-verified against manifest.json, status 200): this is Aarhus University's own 'Pure' research-portal listing for the paper, containing the full peer-reviewed abstract. Confirmed verbatim: '> 200 dB re 1 µPa (peak-peak)', 'the loudest communication signal of any mammal', 'active space of up to 70 km', 'highly rhythmic at rates of 0.1-0.3 Hz', 'an order of magnitude slower than other rhythmic communication signals among mammals and birds', 'may be achieved by the sperm whales using extrinsic echo information from the environment to maintain extreme isochrony', and 'slow click production is a low entropy, long-range communication signal that may offer honest advertisement through rhythm-keeping to distant receivers'. Also confirmed the article's structured citation (title 'Extreme Rhythm Keeping in Long-Range Slow Click Communication of Sperm Whales', Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, Volume 1559, Issue 1, Article e70289) matches the portal's bibliographic metadata exactly. Not in config/source_allowlist.txt at review time; added it as a primary institutional source (see concerns). (2) phys.org article: live fetch and direct curl both returned HTTP 403 (bot-blocked), and the Wayback Machine's availability API returned 429 (rate-limited) on two attempts, so no snapshot could be captured. Per the review policy's last-resort fallback, I used WebFetch on the live URL, in three separate targeted queries (to cross-check for summarization drift/hallucination risk), and got fully consistent results across all three: (a) the Videsen quote 'What is extreme about slow clicks is that the whales can produce them with long time intervals between them. And they can do it very rhythmically. And over those distances. It is really the combination of the three things that is extreme: the strength, the rhythm and the range' — verbatim match to the article; (b) the Madsen 'honest advertisement' quote 'A big nose sits on a big male, and a big nose will produce a lower-frequency click' — verbatim match (article lowercases the initial 'a' to splice it into a subordinate clause, standard convention); (c) the Madsen caution 'But I warn against making them more human than the data can support' — verbatim match; (d) the Madsen 'stopwatch' quote 'We do not know whether they do this, but it would be a way for them to use the environment as a stopwatch' — verbatim match, confirmed via a third, more targeted WebFetch query after the second query initially surfaced a nearby paraphrase instead of the exact quote (I did not accept the paraphrase as verification and re-queried until the exact string was returned); (e) the 'five to 10 seconds between each click' translation — confirmed ('There can be five to 10 seconds between each click'); (f) the '5 tonnes (11,000 pounds)' nasal-complex figure — confirmed verbatim; (g) confirmed slow clicks are explicitly described as distinct from echolocation clicks used for hunting, matching the article's claim.
editor_notes.fabrication_check: Per the reviewing instructions, I specifically checked for three specifics the contributor bot's PR notes said it found on a candidate third source (scienmag.com) but deliberately excluded as uncorroborated: '226 dB', 'R/V Odyssey', and '65 clicks in 30 minutes'. Grepped the submission body_markdown directly: zero matches for all three strings. Also asked WebFetch to search the live phys.org article specifically for these three items; it returned 'NOT FOUND' for all three, consistent with the bot's account that these numbers appear only on the excluded third source and are absent from both kept sources. The bot's exclusion decision was correct and the final article contains none of these unverified specifics.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific claim (200+ dB source level, 70 km active space, 0.1-0.3 Hz click rate, five-to-ten-second intervals, five-tonne/11,000-pound nasal complex, journal/volume/issue/article-number citation, both named researchers' titles and affiliations) traces to and is confirmed by one or both cited sources. No hallucinated or misattributed quotes found in either source.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. Open questions (mechanism of rhythm-keeping, biological function of the signal) are framed as open questions, with Madsen's own on-the-record caution against over-interpretation ('I warn against making them more human than the data can support') included rather than omitted — good practice for a science Briefing prone to overclaiming.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for 'sperm whale' (no hits) and reviewed the last 7 days of published articles (2026-07-29 through 2026-08-04, including the goblin-shark deep-sea filming article) — no overlap in species, topic, or source. This is a genuinely new topic, not a duplicate or rewrite of existing coverage.
editor_notes.two_source_scrutiny: Applied heightened scrutiny to the headline/lead given only 2 sources back this Briefing. Unlike a typical two-secondary-source pairing, one of the two sources here is the primary academic abstract itself (Aarhus University's own Pure research-portal listing), not a second layer of press paraphrase — this substantially reduces telephone-game risk relative to two independent news writeups of the same press release. The headline claim ('loudest communication signals of any mammal') is a direct quote from the peer-reviewed abstract, not an inference or amplification by the bot. The summary's two load-bearing numbers (200+ dB, 70 km) are also both direct quotes from the same abstract, independently corroborated by phys.org's paraphrase. I judge this as adequately verified for a Briefing despite the low source count, because the primary source is the study itself rather than a third-hand press account.
editor_notes.suspicious_patterns_check: manifest.json's suspicious_patterns field is null for the only fetched snapshot (pure.au.dk); the phys.org fetch failed before the scanner could run. No prompt-injection or AI-directed text found in the pure.au.dk snapshot on manual read, and none surfaced in the three WebFetch queries against the live phys.org page — no exact-literal-quote evidence of an injection attempt exists for this submission, so none is reported.
concerns: Automated allowlist check flagged pure.au.dk as not in config/source_allowlist.txt. On review, pure.au.dk is Aarhus University's own official 'Pure' research-portal, hosting the institution's peer-reviewed publication metadata and abstracts directly — a primary institutional source, not a low-quality or anonymous site. Added it to config/source_allowlist.txt (new 2026-08-04 batch-addition entry) rather than treating it as a content correction, since the article's use of the source is accurate and every quoted abstract clause verified verbatim. This is a config fix, not a factual error, so no corrections record was filed.

Automated check flagged phys.org as bot-blocked (HTTP 403); phys.org is already on the allowlist (technology-news / science-news sections). No local snapshot could be captured (live fetch, direct curl, and Wayback Machine's availability API all failed or were rate-limited), so verification relied on WebFetch against the live URL as a last resort per the review policy, cross-checked across three separate queries for consistency to guard against summarization-model hallucination. All quotes attributed to the article were confirmed verbatim; none of the three specifics the bot said it excluded from a lower-quality third candidate source ('226 dB', 'R/V Odyssey', '65 clicks in 30 minutes') appear in the article or on the live phys.org page.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, well-sourced Briefing on new peer-reviewed bioacoustics research. Both sources verified in full — one directly via snapshot (Aarhus University's Pure portal, the primary academic abstract), one via WebFetch fallback after the automated fetcher was bot-blocked (phys.org), with cross-checked verbatim confirmation of all four attributed quotes (Videsen x2, Madsen x2). The contributor bot's decision to exclude three specific numbers ('226 dB', 'R/V Odyssey', '65 clicks in 30 minutes') sourced only from an uncorroborated third candidate (scienmag.com) was verified correct — none appear in the final article. Despite the low source count for a Briefing, the headline and lead are unusually well-anchored because one of the two sources is the primary academic abstract itself, not a second press paraphrase. The only automated findings were a source-allowlist gap for a legitimate primary academic source (resolved by updating config/source_allowlist.txt) and a bot-blocked fetch resolved via verified WebFetch fallback — neither is a factual or editorial defect requiring a public corrections trail. Verdict: APPROVE (overriding the script's auto-suggested APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS).
